paper.title: Definitional or Computational? Decomposing LLM Numeric Fidelity in Financial-Statement Analysis with an XBRL Cascade Oracle

author.affiliation: Université Paris Dauphine - PSL and Bulbshead

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) analyze corporate financial statements fluently, yet routinely emit wrong figures while preserving a confident, well-formatted narrative—the false-precision problem. Prior benchmarks measure answer accuracy or attach claims to source cells, but do not explain why a financial number is wrong. We introduce a deterministic, XBRL-grounded oracle that recomputes the intermediate-management-balances (SIG) and ratio cascade from SEC EDGAR facts, and use it to score numeric fidelity per financial concept, with fact-level attribution and error propagation along the ratio dependency DAG. A pinned/unpinned prompt contrast, an any-standard-definition oracle for convention-dependent composites, and a rule-based error-mode classifier jointly separate definitional divergence (the model applies a different but sometimes valid convention) from unexplained residual numerical error. Across six open and proprietary models on 729 firm-years (and a 345 firm-year subset common to all six), we find: (i) simple two-fact ratios are computed faithfully by all but the weakest model, while multi-input composites separate the panel by capability—the residual hardest concept (ROCE) is executed reliably only by the strongest models; (ii) supplying the exact formula and source tags (pinning) helps every capable model and only hurts the weakest, inverting an apparent "computational limit" that turns out to be a weak-model artifact; and (iii) source-fact attribution and fidelity are distinct and can decouple—one model computes correctly yet cites its source facts almost never ("right answer, no receipts"), while the strongest models pair high fidelity with high attribution. Program-of-thought prompting does not change fidelity, and most wrong composites are local errors rather than propagated ones. Code, frozen model responses and full provenance are released under a DOI.

paper.title: Scripted Hesitation in a Financial Customer-Service Chatbot: A Brazilian Portuguese Case Study
paper.abstract: Financial customer service is a high-stakes conversational domain in which debt negotiation, cancellations, and complaints require pragmatic resources beyond fluent text generation. We present a case study of linguistic hesitation in approximately 3,000 WhatsApp customer-service interaction records (approximately 89k tokens) from one Brazilian financial company, contrasting clients, human agents, and one commercial scripted chatbot. A rule-based pipeline adapted a Conversation Analysis typology to written chat and identified 20,938 pattern occurrences across four formal categories. Client messages account for 59% of detections, but unavailable per-role token totals preclude rate comparisons. Archived within-role distributions place 40% of agent detections in sensitive contexts and 50% of chatbot detections in technical contexts. The chatbot also relies on only 3–5 recurrent surface forms. We interpret these results as descriptive evidence that human and scripted hesitation serve different interactional profiles, not as a general claim about financial chatbots or LLM-based agents. The study illustrates both the value of pragmatic analysis for financial conversational systems and the limits of conclusions drawn from a single-company, single-annotator corpus.

paper.title: FinLCR: Scaling Financial Long-Context Reasoning via Curriculum Reinforcement Learning

author.affiliation: Amazon and University of Minnesota, Minneapolis

paper.abstract: Long-context financial document understanding and reasoning pose significant challenges for small language models (SLMs). In this paper, we scale the financial long-context reasoning capability of SLMs through reinforcement learning. Specifically, we propose an efficient curriculum reinforcement learning recipe that features staged training across context lengths and difficulty-aware data sampling. To support our curriculum recipe, we curate Fin-Ladder, a difficulty-graded financial corpus spanning diverse datasets and context lengths. We apply the proposed corpus and recipe to train Financial Long-Context Reasoner (FinLCR), a 4-billion parameter model with enhanced financial reasoning capabilities. Experiments demonstrate that our curriculum learning recipe yields superior performance on financial numerical reasoning benchmarks.

paper.title: Can LLMs Catch a Rigged Backtest? A Clean-Control Calibration Benchmark
paper.abstract: LLM backtest auditing is a calibration problem: a useful auditor must identify methodology flaws without falsely accusing matched clean strategies. We construct a 96-item paired benchmark in which every flawed backtest has a clean control that holds the strategy, dates, code style, labels, and reporting scaffold fixed while changing one methodology detail. The benchmark covers eight flaw classes, three difficulty strata, prose and code surfaces, and 1,440 cached audits from four smoke-tested text endpoints. A deterministic scorer separately evaluates flaw classification, clean-control false positives, evidence localization, and fix relevance. The primary auditor reaches 100.0% closed and clean-aware code recall, yet open prompts falsely flag 93.8% of clean code controls. A clean-aware warning reduces its code false-positive rate from 20.8% to 0.0% while preserving 100.0% recall, although clean-aware all-three specificity remains 87.5% because some proposed fixes are incomplete. Model behavior differs sharply under the same clean-aware prompt: some models produce no clean false positives, while another flags 38/48 clean controls despite retaining high recall. Reporting recall alone would therefore hide large differences in practical audit quality. The benchmark does not certify live trading systems; it isolates whether an LLM can identify a planted flaw without manufacturing one in a clean counterpart.

paper.title: FinEvo: Financial Language Agents Shape the Markets That Evaluate Them

author.affiliation: Shanghai Innovation Institute and Fudan University
Pengcheng Laboratory and Chinese University of Hong Kong
Shanghai Academy of AI for Science and Fudan University

paper.abstract: Financial language agents are commonly evaluated through static prediction tasks or isolated historical backtests, where an agent’s decisions cannot affect subsequent prices or the behavior of competing strategies. This overlooks a defining property of real markets: interpretations of financial news influence order flow, price formation, and the competitive environment faced by other participants. We introduce FINEVO, a closed-loop evaluation framework that integrates time-stamped financial news, heterogeneous trading agents, a continuous double-auction market, and population-level capital reallocation. FINEVO evaluates language-based agents alongside technical, forecasting, reinforcement-learning, and informed strategies, reporting not only returns but also market concentration, strategic reorganization, regime-dependent standing, and recovery from shocks. Across 128-run suites of controlled market shocks and historical-news-conditioned episodes, we find that language-agent performance is strongly contingent on the surrounding market regime and agent population. Endogenous price formation also causes identical information schedules to produce different outcomes under different competitive compositions. Mechanism ablations further show that innovation is critical for maintaining contestability: removing it increases mean HHI from 0.189 to 0.477 and mean Top-1 capital share from 0.344 to 0.531. These results suggest that financial language agents should be evaluated not only by how accurately they interpret information, but also by how their decisions reshape the markets in which they operate.

paper.title: TRUST-BENCH: A Synthetic Japanese Financial-Group Benchmark for Enterprise Document Access in Coding Agents
paper.abstract: In large financial institutions, what code should do is rarely recoverable from code alone: the authoritative rules live in internal business documents that are largely unreachable to coding agents. Benchmarks built on public repositories therefore cannot measure what reaching those documents is worth. We present TRUST-BENCH, a fully synthetic benchmark that measures the effect of enterprise document availability and of the channel through which it is delivered: the codebase of a fictional Japanese financial group-1,105 programs and 287k lines of code across five languages, a legacy COBOL/PL/I/RPG core of record surrounded by the Java and C periphery paired with 149 Japanese business documents and 93 maintenance tasks. Tasks are graded two ways: an LLM judge scores answers for correctness and completeness, and generated code is compiled, run, and checked against curated test cases.We describe the dataset-generation procedure in detail and report results over four context conditions: code only (the baseline); code with the raw documents on disk; code with documents behind a hybrid retrieval tool; and code with documents behind a knowledge-graph tool. Graph-mediated document access raised retrieval-task correctness from 0.68 to 0.94 while the strict build-task pass rate rose from 27% to 91%.

paper.title: One Advisor, Many Faces: How User Personas Shape LLM Stock Recommendations
paper.abstract: Large language models increasingly act as informal investment advisors, a role that for human professionals is governed by suitability obligations: advice must match the customer’s investment profile (FINRA Rule 2111; SEC Regulation Best Interest, 2019). Whether LLM advice is personalized in this normative sense—or merely stereotyped—is unknown. We audit six model arms from five vendors (2,396 unique single-turn queries, 2026-07-29; four vendors enter inferential analyses) by injecting synthetic user personas manipulating Big Five neuroticism and conscientiousness plus capital size, and score recommended five-stock portfolios against realized market data. Persona effects replicate in every arm analysed inferentially: low conscientiousness raises recommended volatility by 10–25% and increases portfolio beta by 40–96%, while capital size is largely ignored—a suitability inversion. The sign of the neuroticism effect splits across vendors, indicating that models have internalized different stereotypes rather than any consistent normative principle. Removing the stated risk preference amplifies persona spread by 55%, a dose-style signature of stereotype filling. Rationale texts show personas are explicitly mirrored in reasoning, yet this language accounts for under 15% of the behavioral effect: the persona effect resides in portfolio selection rather than in the accompanying rhetoric. We release all logs, prompts, and code.

paper.title: Diagnosing Fine-Grained Inconsistency Classification in Financial Disclosure Text
paper.abstract: Financial disclosures may contain numerical, temporal, referential, factual, and policy inconsistencies that require different evidence and reasoning to diagnose. We study fine-grained inconsistency classification: given a passage known to contain a conflict, the goal is to identify its type among 11 categories. Using a fixed snapshot of the synthetic SBID-FD benchmark, we compare frozen and fine-tuned encoders, evidence-augmented classifiers, prompted large language models, and LoRA-adapted generative models under a shared evaluation protocol. Task-specific adaptation yields large improvements over frozen representations, and a fine-tuned 300M encoder performs competitively with substantially larger prompted and adapted models. We further study whether localizing the conflicting claims improves classification through matched predicted-span, reference-span, and distractor-span conditions. The results show that automatically extracted evidence provides additional signal but recovers only part of the benefit obtained from reference spans. Per-class and confusion analyses further reveal that some inconsistency types are especially sensitive to localization quality, whereas others remain difficult even when the relevant evidence is supplied. These findings identify evidence localization and fine-grained type discrimination as distinct challenges and show that compact supervised encoders are strong baselines for this task.

paper.title: Trust the Query, Not the Answer: Auditable Text-to-SPARQL over the GLEIF Register
paper.abstract: Ask which subsidiaries a conglomerate owns, and a language model returns a plausible list, unverifiable and partly wrong; in compliance or supervision, that will not do. So instead of trusting the answer, a local open-weight model translates each question into an auditable SPARQL query over the GLEIF register, returning the query and its source records. A 20B model answers 86.7% of held-out questions correctly, always with a valid query and declining the unanswerable, and no larger open or closed model does better. The method fits any ontology-described source; code and benchmark are released.

paper.title: MortarBench: Evaluating Mortgage Loan Origination Agents
paper.abstract: Loan origination is the process by which a lender creates a new loan, from application and underwriting through approval and funding. This process serves a critical role in evaluating the eligibility and level of risk posed by an applicant. Recently, firms have begun using mortgage loan agents to augment human loan officers, despite a lack of any public benchmark. To fill this gap, we present MortarBench, a loan origination agent benchmark. MortarBench uses a financial data synthesis and mutation pipeline to generate examples with broad edge case coverage that match real-world distributions and questions. We find that state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) perform poorly, with closed-source models achieving at most 80.8% F1 accuracy. We also discover systematic biases in LLM perception of foreignness related to non-English names. Noting these weaknesses, we introduce CRIT, a confidence calibration framework. Our method increases peak F1 accuracy to 83.6% while improving risk management steering and reducing bias.

paper.title: CARPAS: Towards Content-Aware Refinement of Provided Aspects for Summarization in Large Language Models

author.affiliation: National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University
Department of Computer Science, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University
National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University

paper.abstract: Aspect-based summarization has attracted significant attention for its ability to generate more fine-grained and user-aligned summaries. While most existing approaches assume a set of predefined aspects as input, real-world scenarios often present challenges where these given aspects may be incomplete, irrelevant, or entirely missing from the document. Users frequently expect systems to adaptively refine or filter the provided aspects based on the actual content. In this paper, we initiate this novel task setting, termed Content-Aware Refinement of Provided Aspects for Summarization (CARPAS), with the aim of dynamically adjusting the provided aspects based on the document context before summarizing. We construct three new datasets and conduct pilot experiments with four representative prompting strategies. Our analysis reveals that LLMs often over-generate aspects, resulting in excessively long and misaligned summaries. Building on this observation, we introduce a two-stage framework that derives lightweight scope guidance before aspect refinement and summarization, improving focus and reducing over-generation. Our extensive experiments show that the proposed approach significantly improves performance across all datasets. Moreover, our deeper analyses uncover LLMs’ compliance when the requested number of aspects differs from their own estimations, establishing a crucial insight for the deployment of LLMs in similar real-world applications.

paper.title: What the Window Does Not Contain: Auditing Provenance in a Document-Grounded Instability Benchmark
paper.abstract: Ask a language model the same question about the same document twenty times, and it sometimes returns two different answers. We built Probity, a benchmark of 60 tasks and 470 items from real venture-financing filings, to measure how often this happens. Then we audited our own corpus and found a defect any excerpt-built benchmark can carry: items whose evidence is missing from the window of text the model is shown. The audit flags 36 items and separates two failures a single flag would conflate: evidence genuinely absent from the window, and answers that must be computed from numbers the window does supply. Flagged items change their answers far more often, wobbling at 0.255 against 0.087 on the 427 clean items, and excluding them cuts apparent cross-model agreement by about a fifth. Before testing whether the missing evidence explains the instability, we registered a prediction: re-cut each window to hold its evidence, and instability should fall below a set threshold. It failed: the repair moved wobble by 0.058, with an interval containing zero. We report the association as correlational. Almost all measurements sit where instability cannot show, which bounds what a corpus built for accuracy can say about stability. We release the corpus, all 112,800 raw responses, and the audit as a runnable check for any document benchmark.

paper.title: Auditing Bank Statement PDFs: A Multi-Tier Parser and Design Choices for the NL-to-SQL Query Layer Above It

author.affiliation: Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology

paper.abstract: Bank statements are the primary evidentiary record in financial auditing, yet they reach auditors as heterogeneous PDFs—some digitally typeset, others scanned—transcribed by hand into spreadsheets and interrogated with brittle macros. We describe a system, built with and deployed for an industry partner, that replaces this workflow with (i) a multi-tier parser—a relational data conversion pipeline that routes digital pages to a deterministic table extractor (PyMuPDF) and scanned pages to an OCR/layout service (LlamaParse), standardizes column headers to a canonical schema, and repairs extraction errors with a balance-equation reconciliation engine; and (ii) a natural-language-to-SQL query layer over the resulting database, whose design choices we evaluate by varying context injection. On 23 real statements (20 banks, 1,672 transactions) the pipeline attains 0.9952 transaction-level accuracy. We compare five context-injection strategies across two model generations on 150 auditing queries with hand-authored gold SQL, scored by execution accuracy. Grounding the model on our parser’s structured context consistently helps, whereas raw-text context can degrade accuracy below the Zero-Context baseline; the benefit of self-correcting scaffolding and retrieval, while real, shrinks as the base model improves, so model choice often dominates agent complexity on simple schemas. We release code, two privacy-preserving sample statements, and a sample query set.

paper.title: SpendSight: Privacy-Preserving Personal Finance Q&A with Sub-2B LLMs
paper.abstract: People often speculate about their personal finances: *"Has my spending on groceries increased compared to past year?"*, *"How does my spending on clothes look for the past 6 months?"*. However, answering them with cloud-hosted LLMs transmits sensitive financial data to external servers, exposing users to data leakage and inferential privacy risks. We present **SpendSight**, a study of fully on-device personal finance Q A tool calling that keeps all data strictly local. We evaluate seven quantized models (six sub-2B and one 3B) across 115 test cases and five analytical tools, comparing single-agent against dual-agent (router-specialist) architectures. Dual-agent decomposition yields the largest time gains for the Qwen3.5 family. **Qwen3.5-0.8B** achieves **61.7% Correct Ratio** (**89.1% Task Accuracy**) in **3.0 s** with **1.2 GB RAM** in dual-agent mode. A 3B reference model (**G9v3-3B**, Q4_K_M) achieves **71.7% Correct Ratio** (**90.6% Task Accuracy**) at **2.3 s** in single agent mode, suggesting that larger models with aggressive quantization can bypass decomposition.

paper.title: CORAL: Closed-loop Oracle Alignment for Agentic Tax Engine Modernization
paper.abstract: Modernizing legacy software is often framed as code migration, an approach that assumes access to source code and an understanding of system internals. In practice these assumptions fail: source may be inaccessible, data in proprietary formats, and documentation dispersed. We study an underexplored regime in which a replacement is aligned to a legacy system treated as a black-box oracle, using only its input–output behavior.We present CORAL (Closed-loop Oracle Alignment), an agentic framework that aligns a modern U.S. individual income tax engine (Form 1040) to a production oracle (a system built over decades) by iteratively refining LLM-bootstrapped form schemas. Each round runs a scenario on both systems, compares e-file output field-by-field, and diagnoses discrepancies against an authoritative IRS knowledge base (KB), grounding every fix in published regulation rather than relying on model knowledge. An edit is kept only if re-execution shows no meaningful field-level F_1 regression and all tests pass, a deterministic check rather than model self-assessment. Round-robin sequencing over under-covered forms then reaches the long tail of forms, not just the high-frequency ones a taxpayer shares with everyone.Across 119 tax-expert-authored scenarios, each a complete taxpayer return, CORAL repairs defects from single-field corrections to reviving entire non-functional forms (53 fixed; 13 escalated to human review, ensuring ambiguous rules and input-data gaps are audited manually), lifting macro-F_1 on a 30-scenario held-out test split, averaged over returns, from an LLM-bootstrapped start (0.17) to 0.90.

paper.title: What Deterministic Verification Actually Fixes in Financial QA: A Diagnostic Analysis of Rule Heterogeneity Across Datasets
paper.abstract: Deterministic, parameter-free post-hoc correction rules are an attractive way to address numerical errors in financial question answering: they are simple, cheap, and fully auditable. We ask whether such rules actually behave like general-purpose correctors, or whether their effect is contingent on properties of the dataset and model output distribution they are applied to. We evaluate a two-rule deterministic verification layer (DVL) — scale_mul100 and scale_div100 — on FinQA (n=873) and TAT-QA (n=718) using Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3. This same, fixed model-plus-rule configuration produces a striking cross-dataset divergence: harmful on FinQA (37.34%→16.04%, −21.31pp, McNemar p=1.76×10⁻³⁹) and beneficial on TAT-QA (26.32%→30.64%, +4.32pp, p=5.15×10⁻³). A rule-level transition analysis shows scale_mul100 is highly precise on TAT-QA (87.95%) but overwhelmingly imprecise on FinQA (3.39%), while scale_div100 produces zero observed corrections and only harm in both settings; removing it raises TAT-QA accuracy further, to 35.10%. We do not find evidence that these rules correct arithmetic, retrieval, or semantic reasoning failures. We conclude that this specific pair of scaling rules is better understood as a targeted, dataset-contingent representation normalizer than as a general reasoning corrector, and we characterize the boundary conditions under which it helps or hurts.

paper.title: Where A Small Language Model Helps in Invoice Categorisation, Understood Through Embedding Geometry
paper.abstract: Categorising invoices into the correct General Ledger (GL) code underpins financial reporting and tax compliance. This is a skilled accounting judgement rather than a routine task: the correct category depends subtly on the nature of the purchasing business, the vendor and the invoice text. Whilst AI is increasingly being adopted across industries to automate tasks, including invoice categorisation, implementations built on in-house small language models (SLMs) can simultaneously reduce cost and improve data security, confidentiality, and interpretability. We investigate this approach by first analysing the pre-trained embedding geometry of a small sentence transformer (SBERT) and classic SLM (DeBERTa). The sentence-embedding space of this financial corpus is globally anisotropic but composed of locally isotropic clusters, extending prior token-level findings to sentence embeddings in a financial setting, and these clusters are strongly correlated with the vendor identity. SBERT fine-tuned on a single GPU reaches 0.96 accuracy on invoice classification, above both a zero-shot locally deployable LLM and a vendor identity baseline, increasing performance for smaller, challenging categories and new clients. For this important generalisation problem, SBERT reaches 0.9 F1 with roughly 100 client-specific invoices, showing that an in-house SLM implementation is promising. Combining these results with geometric analysis shows that pre-trained embedding geometry is associated with classification performance and reveals a counterintuitive finding that a structured input that would help a human reader does not improve the SLM performance.

paper.title: FinDRA: Multi-Agent Financial Reasoning under Asymmetric Information and Unequal Authority
paper.abstract: We propose FinDRA, a multi-agent framework for financial question answering under asymmetric information access. FinDRA partitions a financial report into agent-specific evidence regions, allows agents to exchange only their answers, concise reasoning, and confidence estimates, and coordinates their revisions through full-document verifier feedback and authority-framed debate. Experiments on MultiHiertt show that the asymmetric verifier condition obtains the highest overall point estimates among the compared settings, with an EM score of 0.284 and a mean LLM-as-a-Judge score of 0.753 on a 0–2 scale. Importantly, the benefit of asymmetric access depends on evidence structure: it is strongest when question-relevant evidence remains within an agent-accessible region, whereas cross-partition questions expose a trade-off between semantic adequacy and exact numerical agreement. Agent-level analyses further show revision patterns consistent with the assigned authority framing, without attributing these differences to authority alone. Cross-dataset experiments on FinQA and TAT-QA similarly show that asymmetric access is not universally beneficial. These findings suggest that effective multi-agent financial reasoning depends not simply on providing more information, but on how evidence is partitioned, communicated, and verified.

paper.title: FRED-SemBench: Evaluating Semantic Reliability in LLM Access to Macroeconomic Data
paper.abstract: Access to authoritative financial data does not ensure semantically correct answers: a language model may retrieve a valid observation associated with the wrong series, transformation, unit, or temporal interpretation. We introduce FRED-SemBench, a 200-question benchmark candidate over independently selected Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED) concepts that separates retrieval failures from semantic data-access failures. We also instantiate Iris, an ontology-backed semantic layer whose versioned concept contracts bind user intent to provider series, transformations, units, temporal semantics, provenance, and declared coverage. A controlled comparison of an unaided model, FRED and Web access, and Iris reveals a reliability trade-off: raw retrieval substantially improves numerical answering while suppressing abstention and reducing clarification accuracy on underspecified queries. Within its pre-declared support set, Iris preserves the numerical benefit, restores clarification behavior, and attains the strongest strict accuracy, suggesting that this trade-off is not intrinsic to data access. These pilot findings motivate evaluating macroeconomic data access jointly in terms of semantic correctness, boundary behavior, coverage, and operational cost.

paper.title: BankShield: Fairness-Aware Safety Guardrails for Indian-Language Banking AI
paper.abstract: Safety guards for Indian-language banking must detect discrimination without changing verdicts solely because a demographic identity changes. We introduce GuardAudit, an evaluation protocol combining decontamination, paired harmful/benign calibration, counterfactual identity tests, and deployed-action evaluation, plus two released banking benchmarks. Across six guards, the hardest matched test remains unresolved: the best system flags a coded proxy denial while clearing its matched actuarial control on only 37.5% of pairs. BankShield, used as a case study, reaches 20.0% and false-flags 75.0% of expert-validated legitimate controls. On separate BharatBBQ subsets, it achieves 0% flip on benign identity substitutions and 66.7% biased-content catch; these disjoint measurements do not establish joint per-example fairness. Its unadapted 12B backbone supplies near-invariance and attack recall, while adaptation and a discrimination probe raise biased-content catch from 24% to 43% and 66.7%, not significantly above a smaller Indic guard’s 56.9% (p=0.09). Detection also falls from 81.6% in English to 42.6% in Devanagari Hindi. BankShield is therefore a diagnostic case study, not a deployment-ready fairness solution. We release the protocol, benchmarks, and frozen predictions.

paper.title: NLP for Crowdfunding Success Prediction: A Systematic Mapping Review Exposes an Underexplored Equity Domain
paper.abstract: Equity crowdfunding under U.S. Regulation Crowdfunding (Reg CF) raised over 1.4 billion across 5,969 offerings between May 2016 and December 2022 (Chang, 2024), generating a large public corpus of Form C business descriptions on SEC EDGAR. Yet regulated equity crowdfunding remains barely studied by the financial NLP community. We conduct a systematic mapping review using automated database search, independent dual-LLM screening, targeted human adjudication, and blind quality-control auditing. We screened 726 deduplicated papers and included 49 studies applying NLP directly to crowdfunding campaign text. Only one study examines U.S. Reg CF campaign text directly, using readability, with one pre-Reg-CF Title II near-neighbor using sentiment tone and description length. The available equity-crowdfunding evidence is therefore too limited and heterogeneous to support general conclusions about the strength of textual signals in regulated equity settings. We taxonomize the included studies into five NLP method families, synthesize representative cross-study evidence in the original reported units, and identify the near absence of regulated equity research across the methodological spectrum. We also discuss regulatory constraints, structured financial information, and text length as plausible but untested explanations for this gap. The annotated evidence base, screening records, and reproducibility materials are publicly available at https://github.com/jct-nlp/finNLP-crowdfunding

paper.title: When Words Move Markets: Sentiment and Semantic Complexity in Central Bank Communication and Equity Volatility

author.affiliation: International Institute of Information Technology Hyderabad, Dhirubhai Ambani Institute Of Information and Communication Technology

paper.abstract: Central bank communications influence market expectations, but their linguistic attributes are inadequately examined in emerging markets. We examine 337 Reserve Bank of India Monetary Policy Committee documents (2010–2025) and relate their textual features to minute-level and daily volatility in NIFTY indices. Our load-bearing result concerns sentiment. Within a pre-specified nine-test confirmatory family, negative-sentiment probability is associated with event-window equity volatility and CLS-based sentiment with event-window turbulence in India VIX; both survive Benjamini–Hochberg correction, rank correlation, bootstrap intervals and regime-conditional controls, both strengthen under a time-matched volatility baseline, and both outperform a Loughran–McDonald lexicon on an identical sample. The sentiment model is a fine-tuned FinBERT that we validate directly on human-annotated central-bank text (81.3% accuracy, macro-F_1 = 0.784, Cohen’s \kappa = 0.714 against a human majority vote). Semantic complexity, measured with the DAST framework, plays a secondary, construct-level role: it is largely orthogonal to classical readability (|r|_{\max}=0.21) but behaves as an ordinal measure of generated semantic structure, and at the daily horizon a sentiment\timescomplexity interaction yields only small exploratory in-sample gains that are not significant under heteroskedasticity-robust inference and do not improve out-of-sample prediction, even after controlling for document length. A third candidate, attention concentration, is Bonferroni-significant under Pearson correlation yet reverses sign under Spearman and has a bootstrap interval spanning zero; we report it as a cautionary methodological result rather than a finding. A pre-specified February 20 Chow test and an endogenous break search near March 11, 2020 indicate pronounced COVID-period regime dependence. Overall, textual features add in-sample explanatory power over a GARCH plus policy-rate baseline but no incremental out-of-sample predictive value on any index.

paper.title: Same Financials, Different Identity: A Counterfactual Audit of Demographic Sensitivity in LLM-Based Credit-Risk Scoring

author.affiliation: TÜBİTAK (Türkiye Bilimsel ve Teknolojik Araştırma Kurumu)
TÜBİTAK (Türkiye Bilimsel ve Teknolojik Araştırma Kurumu)

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are being explored as decision-support tools for financial risk assessment. Their outputs may, however, respond to demographic descriptions that are unrelated to the underlying financial record. We study this behavior through a paired counterfactual audit. The same 100 commercial credit and cheque-payment profiles are evaluated repeatedly, with only one demographic descriptor changed at a time. The experiments cover 7 model variants, three prompting strategies, and descriptors related to gender, education, and citizenship. While paired gender score differences remain within a \pm1.5 point equivalence margin in 12 of 21 model–strategy cells, education shows a strong, unambiguous effect. Risk decreases monotonically with education level (103 of 126 pairwise contrasts remain significant after Holm correction, score differences reaching 26.0 points between primary-school and doctorate descriptors), it flips up to 42% of approve/reject decisions, and elicited rationales name education as a risk factor even though education is not a financially legitimate predictor. Citizenship produces larger shifts still, flipping up to 51% of decisions while leaving AUC almost unchanged in most cells, and in one model weakening ranking (0.794 to 0.438). Similar to education, rationales name the descriptor as the reason. Unlike citizenship, whose jurisdictional cues can legitimately enter sanctions or AML/CFT screening, the education effect has no such justification, making it the clearest evidence of demographic bias. A follow-up experiment in English, Chinese, and Arabic shows that citizenship sensitivity depends on both prompt language and prompting strategy, affecting the magnitude and direction of score shifts. The study provides a standardized counterfactual framework for auditing LLM-generated scores before they are considered for high-stakes financial workflows.

paper.title: CAST: An Interpretable Evidence-Based Confidence Estimation Tool for RAG with Human-in-the-Loop Verification
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly assist financial analysis tasks over filings, reports, and news via retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), but a human reviewer typically remains accountable for the final decision. In this setting, a confidence score must be more than well-calibrated: it must be evidence-based and explainable, so reviewers can see why an answer should be trusted. We introduce CAST (Confidence via Answer Support Testing), a Bayesian-inspired confidence method that compares a generated answer with a plausible competing alternative and evaluates how retrieved passages support each hypothesis. CAST produces both an answer-level confidence score and citation-level evidence for review. We also demonstrate CAST through an interactive reviewer-facing tool that visualizes supporting and opposing evidence for human verification. On 1,286 financial-report questions from MMDocRAG, CAST achieves the highest AUROC among seven evaluated methods (0.634 vs. 0.598 for the strongest baseline).

paper.title: GRPO for Financial Advice Generation: Outperforming Commercial LLMs under CATE Evaluation

author.affiliation: Intuit and Ben Gurion University of the Negev

paper.abstract: Generating actionable financial advice from business records demands that models integrate numerical reasoning, domain knowledge, and sound judgment, while avoiding recommendations that could harm the business. Direct supervision is difficult: historical decisions are not necessarily optimal, and high-quality free-form labels are expensive to obtain. We formulate financial advice generation as a reinforcement learning problem and fine-tune an open-weight language model using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Our reward is an LLM-as-a-judge rubric that scores each recommendation across multiple binary dimensions of advice quality, augmented with a safety gate for harm prevention.Since LLM-based evaluation alone cannot confirm whether improvements reflect genuine business value rather than adaptation to the judge, we complement it with a judge-independent audit based on a standard doubly-robust Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) estimator. Under this observational off-policy audit, our trained LLM achieves approximately twice the estimated gross-profit lift of the strongest evaluated commercial baseline (0.0228 vs. 0.0104), together with the lowest downside rate and the least negative tail risk of any policy evaluated. Notably, the two evaluations do not rank the baselines identically: the untrained base model places last on the judge rubric but second on the causal audit, indicating that the audit captures a signal the judge does not. Our results demonstrate that GRPO with a finance-grounded reward signal can produce substantially more useful business recommendations than commercial LLMs, and that a judge-independent causal audit is a valuable complement to, rather than a confirmation of, LLM-as-a-judge assessment in financial NLP.

paper.title: LatentDemandBench: A Contamination-Resistant Diagnostic for Pre-Recognition Product–Need Ranking in Synthetic Economies
paper.abstract: An existing product may meet an unmet need before the market recognises the connection. Testing whether a language model can identify such opportunities is difficult when historical outcomes may already be in its training data. We introduce LatentDemandBench, a contamination-resistant benchmark that generates fictional economies with known realisation probabilities and noisy documentary evidence. Solvers rank product–need pairings by their chance of realisation within a fixed horizon. Market commentary is generated separately from realisation, allowing us to evaluate ranking both among discussed pairings and where market attention supplies no ordering. On 30 matched economies, two frontier models beat a mention-count control but trail a supervised logistic ranker using fourteen features recovered from the same dossiers by a template-aware parser. The stronger model, GPT-5.6-TERRA, scores 0.669 in top-K-imputed AUC, with a paired reference-minus-model gap of +0.047 [+0.025, +0.074]. Aggregating three completions under the same final top-K budget yields 0.659, leaving a reference gap of +0.058 [+0.031, +0.095]. The deficit is not uniform: an exploratory analysis finds it smaller on unmentioned pairings than on those already discussed. We release the generator, harness and artifacts to support evaluation on fresh economies

paper.title: What Ensemble Brier Scores Hide: Evidence Routing at a Fixed Article-Exposure Budget in LLM Prediction-Market Forecasting
paper.abstract: We ask whether giving different evidence to different LLM forecasters creates useful diversity when the total article-exposure count is held fixed. Across 708 resolved prediction-market contracts, we compare six-member ensembles whose forecasters either share the same two article pair or are distributed evenly across three pairs, with both conditions using twelve article exposures. On 609 pre-market-end contracts, evidence routing reliably increases within-ensemble dispersion for GPT-4.1-mini, Qwen3-30B, and OLMo-3.1-32B. An exact Brier-score decomposition separates changes in member error, dispersion, and ensemble error, while a grouped-variance analysis attributes nearly all of the dispersion increase to differences between assigned article pairs rather than repeated sampling. Greater dispersion, however, does not automatically improve the en- semble: only Qwen’s reduction in ensemble Brier survives multiplicity correction, while GPT and OLMo show no statistically robust net improvement. Post-hoc controls show that more balanced routing further increases dispersion at a fixed evidence union, while an alterna- tive Qwen readout changes channel attribution without establishing a different net effect. Evidence routing therefore consistently increases forecast diversity in this setting, but its value depends on whether that diversity outweighs any loss in individual forecast quality.

paper.title: Continuous Financial Knowledge Graph Construction with Citation-Grounded Agentic Question Answering
paper.abstract: Financial analysis requires crossing evidence modalities that arrive in incompatible forms — structured market data, reported text (news and regulatory filings), collective expectations from prediction markets, and private portfolio state — which existing systems either handle in isolation or collapse into a single index, destroying the distinction between observed measurements, attributed claims, probabilistic beliefs, and user-specific exposure. We present a continuously running financial NLP system that maintains these modalities natively, linked by canonical entities and time, through continuous knowledge graph construction with per-edge provenance and temporal decay, and answers questions via agentic tool use under a citation contract that is enforced structurally: every citation must resolve to a passage retrieved in the same session, and free-text figures must agree with provider-attributed tool outputs. A learned relevance gate formalises the extraction cost/quality tradeoff, reducing LLM extraction calls while retaining the majority of yield-positive documents. Over 284 benchmark questions executed three times under majority vote, 251 produce non-failing responses (205 strong, 20 pass, 26 weak), 23 fail, and 10 additional questions are data-absent under the evaluation protocol. A structural evaluation framework of eight deterministic pre-judge gates reaches κ = 0.860 with a human annotator. In a sample evaluation, grounding entity descriptions in retrieved passages cuts fabrication from 1.83 to 0.17 unverifiable claims per description.

paper.title: Relevant Is Not Enough: Expert-Audited Decision-Grade Web Evidence for Financial Fact Verification
paper.abstract: Fact verification systems rank web evidence by relevance, yet relevant passages may lack verdict-critical facts. We define decision-grade evidence as credible, temporally valid, and claim-matched information independently sufficient to support or refute a claim. Using 750 expert-audited claim–passage pairs for 150 financial claims, we compare relevance and decision-grade supervision within two rerankers while holding candidate evidence pools and verifiers fixed. Within these pools, 66.5% of relevant pairs are insufficient, and claim-level decision-grade coverage trails relevance coverage by 40.0 percentage points. Compared with relevance supervision, decision-grade supervision improves the ranking of sufficient evidence in one reranker but shows no clear advantage in the other. Frozen (untuned) rerankers remain competitive, and downstream verification gains are modest and input-dependent. Thus, relevance is an unreliable proxy for verdict sufficiency; evidence availability, ordering, and verifier use require separate evaluation.

paper.title: Helping Customers in Distress: An LLM-powered Agent that Converses, Probes, and Routes
paper.abstract: Banks receive millions of reports of fraud, scams, and disputed transactions every year, making it challenging to accurately direct customers to the appropriate specialist teams for assistance. The existing manual process driven by humans is slow and stressful for both customers and staff. To address this, we develop a customer-facing AI powered triaging agent that leverages large language models (LLMs) to conduct multi-turn conversations, ask relevant questions, and classify cases for accurate, policy-guided routing, making it embedded in the customer journey. To evaluate and continuously improve the agent, synthetic digital twins of real customers were simulated, generating realistic, labelled dialogues based on historical data to test a wide range of real-world scenarios. This work details the triage agent’s modelling approach, integration with policy, safety guardrails and reasoning frameworks, the use of the synthetic agent for scalable evaluation, and findings on the AI system’s accuracy, robustness, and compliance. Results show that the agent successfully improves triaging of historical cases, achieving a 30.6% increase in classification accuracy, with high satisfaction levels reported by our subject-matter experts, highlighting how targeted probing can lead to more effective triage in banking operations at scale.‘

paper.title: Beyond Compressibility: Transferable Low-Dimensional Structure and the Limits of Compression in Financial Retrieval
paper.abstract: Modern retrieval embeddings are highly compressible, often retaining most of their effectiveness after the removal of a large fraction of dimensions. This suggests that retrieval-relevant information is organized in a lower-dimensional structure, but it remains unclear how broadly that structure generalizes and what ultimately limits compression.We study this question in long-document financial retrieval where relevant evidence must be distinguished from many highly similar passages containing repeated entities, financial metrics, tables, and boilerplate. Across three financial retrieval benchmarks and eight retrievers, we find that PCA projections learned on one corpus transfer effectively to others, retaining most of the effectiveness of corpus-specific fitting. Transfer quality is strongly associated with principal-subspace overlap, consistent with substantial shared low-dimensional structure across financial corpora. We further show that global geometric measures such as intrinsic dimension only partially explain retrieval robustness under dimensionality reduction. A case study on a financial question answering benchmark links retrieval failures to dense clusters of competing table chunks: Removing these distractors substantially reduces performance degradation. These results suggest that transferability is enabled by low-dimensional structure that generalizes across financial corpora, while compression failures are associated with local retrieval competition that is not captured by existing global geometric measures.

paper.title: Same Meaning, Different Wording: Evaluating Paraphrase Robustness in Financial Natural Language Inference
paper.abstract: We present FinNLI-Para, a paraphrased version of financial natural language inference (FinNLI). We investigate how much predictions on FinNLI depend on the particular wording used to express a financial hypothesis. We generate three paraphrases for each FinNLI hypothesis and use them to test prediction consistency across eleven model–prompt configurations. Models change their predictions on 7.9–12.3% of paraphrased examples, despite 98.35% of paraphrases preserving the original NLI label, indicating that financial NLI systems remain sensitive to hypothesis wording.

paper.title: Regression-Aware Statistically Gated Policy Updating for Korean Financial LLM Input Guardrails

author.affiliation: Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology and Financial Security Institute
Ewha Women's University and DATUMO Inc.

paper.abstract: Financial institutions must prevent personally identifiable information (PII) and adversarial instructions from entering large language models (LLMs). We present regression-aware policy maintenance for Korean financial LLM input guardrails, supported by a cost-ordered Regex–NER–LLM cascade. On a privacy-preserving controlled set of 1,000 synthetic attacks and 200 routine requests, four manual iterations reduce in-distribution attack success rate (ASR) from 8.9% to 0.3% with a 0.5% false-positive rate (FPR) on the original tuning set. On a held-out split, a policy tuned only on the tuning split achieves 0/300 attack successes and 1/60 false positives, with Wilson 95% CIs of [0, 1.26]% and [0.29, 8.86]%, respectively. For policy maintenance, an LLM generates candidate patches, while paired McNemar tests, an FPR constraint, and cumulative regression checks determine acceptance or rejection. Paired regression testing detects an intermediate regression introduced in manual Round 3, while the gate rejects all five automatically generated candidates, preventing statistically unsupported changes from entering the policy. For boundary diagnosis, the rejected fifth-round candidate yields a pre-mitigation overall FPR of 28.9% across 350 benign examples, including 150 hard negatives, revealing context-blind Regex blocking and LLM-judge over-blocking hidden by routine benign requests. These results support regression-aware policy maintenance in the controlled setting while highlighting the need for broader boundary and deployment-specific evaluation.

paper.title: Characterizing Ambiguity in Financial Document Question Answering

author.affiliation: University of North Carolina at Charlotte

paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in question answering (QA) over general knowledge. However, naturally occurring ambiguity in text poses significant challenges. Users may omit important contextual information from their queries, available context may be insufficient to answer a question without making assumptions, while frontier models tend to give confident answers rather than ask clarifying questions. Research on ambiguity in QA has focused primarily on factoid and general-knowledge settings that rely on LLM-internal knowledge, leaving a gap in research on domain-specific and document QA.We examine how natural ambiguity arises in financial document QA, focusing on hybrid documents containing both text and tables. To this aim, we annotate 200 questions sampled from the MultiHiertt dataset and find that 77% of them exhibit some degree of ambiguity, with 52% of that ambiguity at least partially due to the data itself. We propose an extended taxonomy that accounts for ambiguity source (document vs. query) and degree. Upon evaluating frontier LLMs on ambiguity detection, we observe sharp drops in accuracy across the ambiguity spectrum and high false positive rates. Additionally, inter-model agreement is low, suggesting that models lack a consistent notion of ambiguity.

paper.title: How LLM Financial Agents Respond to Stated Affect Depends on Their Assigned Role

author.affiliation: National Taiwan University and National Taiwan University

paper.abstract: We test whether financial LLM agents respond differently to reports with identical facts, forecasts and recommendations but different wording. The reports differ only in a closing sentence stating the sender’s affect. The most consistent finding is linguistic: high-arousal wording increases readers’ word-based arousal scores on average and also changes teammates’ language. The response varies across rolespecific task instructions, although its magnitude and ordering change across prompt paraphrases, scoring methods, word-removal controls and model families. The central role comparison contains 7,080 generations, but all concern one underlying deposit-outflow event; the 59 matched pairs are seeded realizations of the same financial payload rather than independent financial situations. Separately varying alarm and urgency shows that both raise word-based arousal, while alarmed wording adds an apprehension component detected by an emotion classifier. Behavioral effects are less consistent: in the primary model, alarmed wording reduces adherence to BUY and SELL recommendations, but the SELL reported-size effect is not detected in two additional model families. A filter that removes explicit alarm while preserving checked financial fields leaves most of the linguistic response intact.

paper.title: Preliminary Study on LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluation of Causal Mechanism Explanations in Financial News and its Bias Analysis
paper.abstract: Evaluating causal mechanism explanations in generated financial news is challenging because stock price movements may have multiple plausible explanations without a unique gold explanation. We propose a reference-free LLM-as-a-Judge framework that evaluates explanations from three perspectives: Relevance, Completeness, and Economic Plausibility. We construct 200 articles from Chinese stock market data and compare Gemini 3.5 Flash, GPT-5.5, and Claude Opus 5 with human annotations under zero-shot and few-shot settings. Before aggregating the evaluation results, we applied a systematic matched-subset procedure to examine potential self-preference and generation-source bias. Based on the data examined in this study, these analyses found no statistically significant evidence of systematic bias, supporting the aggregation of all 200 articles for the overall agreement analysis. The results show moderate to high agreement with human evaluation, with Completeness generally showing higher agreement than Relevance. Few-shot prompting does not consistently improve agreement and generally leads to more conservative judgments. These findings demonstrate the potential of LLM-as-a-Judge for reference-free evaluation of causal mechanism explanations in financial news.

paper.title: Valid but Wrong: Domain Invariants and a Cross-Model Plan-Validity Benchmark for Household-Finance LLMs
paper.abstract: Today’s LLMs are good at solving scoped financial tasks. A plan may be type-correct, schema-valid, and executable, yet not financially sound: double-spending the same dollar, or leaving free employer-match money on the table. We call these valid but wrong, and show that today’s evaluations do not consider them. We contribute: (1) a validity hierarchy separating syntactic, schematic, and executional validity from domain validity; (2) a succinct list of domain invariants operationalizing this idea for household finance, divided into conservation and efficiency invariants, grounded in a real six-figure failure in a deployed system; (3) a cross-model measure: we ask eleven current LLMs to plan out a balanced scenario bank (N=585 surface-valid plans) and evaluate each using our invariants. All conform to type, schema, and execution, yet a nonzero fraction break domain invariants which escape detection in surface validity checks. We distinguish a dominance violation over capturable match (unassailable) from an instruction-following violation (does-it-sum) and a contested idle-cash violation. Pooled rates of violating unassailable invariants (the "floor") are 15.2% (95% CI 12–18%), driven by two small models and by instruction-following; the dominance-only floor is 6.2% pooled and 3.6% for the nine frontier models, whose per-model floors overlap. However, the best model (GPT-5) breaks no unassailable invariants, but parks cash idle on 41% of plans, while a small deployable model fails basic conservation 85% of the time. A median 2,500 in guaranteed employer match is tossed aside per dominance violation. Floors hold even on trap-free controls (7.6\%). Using a tighter definition counting idle cash, which is a preference-based decision, we find an upper bound of 51.3\%. Capability improves on conservation errors but does not close the gap on domain validity.

paper.title: CLAIR-Fin: An Adversarial Multi-Agent Framework for Claim-Level Verification and Adaptive Debate in Cross-Modal Financial QA

author.affiliation: Jashore University of Science and Technology
Jashore University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Existing defenses against hallucination in retrieval-augmented and multi-agent pipelines remain partial: evidence is trusted despite modality disagreement, debate verifies an aggregate report rather than individual claims, and such verification occurs only after drafting, leaving inter-agent errors undetected until the final text. To close this gap, we present CLAIR-Fin, a nine-agent framework that decomposes each question into atomic claims maintained in a typed Financial Claim Ledger. Each claim is resolved through Asymmetric Evidence Authority, which conditions evidence trust on claim type rather than treating all modalities as equally reliable; Chain-of-Custody Verification, which checks grounding at the hand-off between drafting and adversarial review rather than only at the pipeline’s exit; an Adaptive Rebuttal Cycle, which routes contested claims through adversarial debate whose depth scales with what that debate finds; and a terminal entailment audit paired with a continuous Hallucination Risk Index that distinguishes claims that passed scrutiny from claims never contested. We evaluate CLAIR-Fin on BB-FinQA-X, a 500-question cross-modal financial evaluation set built from Bangladesh Bank Annual Report material, stratified by query type, format, and difficulty. Relative to a single-pass retrieval-augmented generation baseline, it raises faithfulness (0.780 \rightarrow 0.889) while abstaining on 5.4% of questions when evidence is insufficient rather than forcing an unsupported response, and it exceeds stronger retrieval-strategy baselines such as HyDE and Graph-RAG on faithfulness (\leq 0.874).

paper.title: When FEVER Meets Finance: A Controlled Benchmark Reveals Overlap-Driven Financial Claim Verification
paper.abstract: Realistic financial misinformation is typically a single-token edit of a true statement, yet no public financial dataset supports per-edit statements about which factual changes a verification system can detect. We introduce a controlled benchmark of 1,489 claim-evidence pairs derived from SEC 10-K filings via documented FactCC-style perturbations (number changes, negation flips, entity swaps, evidence mismatches), each pair tagged with its generation rule, and use it to evaluate eleven models spanning three technological generations - TF-IDF linear classifiers, tree ensembles, and neural models including a fine-tuned transformer - all trained on FEVER under one protocol. Per-edit attribution is our central result: the strongest model verifies verbatim financial claims at 98.8% accuracy but detects single-token falsifications at 33% accuracy or below, with number changes and negation flips detected at similar rates and entity swaps far the hardest (2.6%, on 38 pairs). Two diagnoses follow. A hypothesis-only probe shows the classical tier’s in-domain competence is claim-surface artifact - a claim-only classifier reaches macro-F1 0.556 against 0.549 for full claim+evidence models - while our benchmark shows no such artifact under the same probe (0.358). And transfer to real financial claims collapses: on Fin-Fact, no learned model beats a tuned lexical-overlap heuristic (macro-F1 0.368), despite in-domain scores up to 0.841. We release the benchmark, generation code, and evaluation harness.

paper.title: Perceived Professionalism in Financial Inquiry: An Interpretable and Empirically Grounded Linguistic Modeling of Textual Preference
paper.abstract: Professionalism is a central yet underdefined aspect of expert communication. This study investigates whether perceived professionalism can be modeled computationally in financial Q A contexts, and whether non-expert preferences provide a meaningful basis for its annotation. We compile a mixed dataset of real and synthetically generated questions from earnings calls, annotated with human judgments of perceived professionalism and linguistically motivated features. Regression and classification experiments show that these features effectively capture evaluators’ preferences, enabling simple models to outperform both text-only and LLM baselines. The results demonstrate that interpretable, conceptually grounded linguistic features can rival more complex architectures while providing greater transparency, and support the value of linguistic awareness in NLP. More broadly, the study shows that modeling reader preferences can offers insights for the generation of professional questions.

paper.title: Selective Compliance in Financial Rule Reasoning: A Solver-Verified Chinese Benchmark and Empirical Analysis
paper.abstract: Selective compliance is important for financial LLM applications: an applicable context rule should override the LLM’s parametric rule, while an inapplicable rule should be ignored. Though previous studies recognize the importance of rule selection, dedicated evaluations tailored specifically to the financial domain remain absent. To bridge this gap, we build a controlled benchmark based on the CFLUE dataset, where intervention rules are synthesized and FOL logic is applied to ensure the correctness of the new derived answer. Furthermore, we designed three evaluation settings covering clean inputs, noisy inputs, and multi-hop reasoning scenarios. We conduct a systematic comparison across different rule selection strategies and models. Experiments show that: (1) For recent advanced LLMs, single-pass integrated reasoning approach (CAR-Joint) consistently outperforms the decoupled ‘route-then-answer’ approach (CAR-Route). (2) Our proposed post-hoc review method, CAR-Joint-Review, consistently outperforms CAR-Joint. Similarly, pre-hoc routing via the parametric rule elicitation method CAR-Elicit-Route surpasses CAR-Route in multi-hop settings. The performance gains are model-dependent. These findings reveal the trade-offs across various methods and LLMs in financial selective compliance.

paper.title: Hidden Below the Landing Page: Tracking Linked Pages and Relation-Centered DOM Summaries for Financial Phishing Detection

author.affiliation: Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology and Financial Security Institute
Ewha Women's University and DATUMO Inc.

paper.abstract: Phishing can turn stolen personal information into financial harm, yet some sites hide data collection beyond the landing page. We present a site-level workflow for Korean-language phishing that tracks linked pages and supplies LLMs with relation-centered DOM summaries. The 256 landing URLs treated as phishing in the full collection were labeled primarily by the initial LLM, with human labels taking precedence for reviewed sites. Of these, 161 (62.9%) were detected by at least one VirusTotal engine; 215 of 217 linked URLs (99.1%) had no prior query record, and neither remaining URL was detected. On 70 human-validated landing pages, summarization increased Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite’s F1 from 0.621 to 0.925, while F1 changes for the other three Gemini models ranged from -0.011 to +0.035. In a six-site case study, data collection was detected only on linked pages, while page-level aggregation retained landing-page impersonation targets more consistently than concatenation. These results highlight the importance of exploration scope and show model-dependent accuracy effects of relation-centered DOM summaries in phishing detection.

paper.title: Prediction-Market Seed Capital Recovery from Noise-Dominant Flow

author.affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence and McGill University

paper.abstract: Automated prediction markets require sponsors to prefund liquidity before observing order flow, creating a financing challenge at launch. We study whether nonnegative charges conditioned on observable payoff direction can improve recovery of this prefunded capital while limiting their effect on informed participation. We develop Seed Capital Flow (SCF), a direction-conditioned levy, in a stylized binary cost- function market with informed and liquidity-motivated traders. When order composition differs across directions, SCF concentrates the permitted fee burden on the direction with relatively more liquidity-motivated flow, whereas a uniform fee spreads it across both directions. Under a common retention constraint, this allocation yields higher expected recovery capacity and can make additional liquidity choices financially viable. Synthetic numerical audits examine robustness to alternative flow patterns, stochastic arrivals, and label misspecification. The results characterize a mechanism-design tradeoff rather than an empirical prediction: the market remains prefunded, recovery is expected rather than guaranteed, and the analysis is limited to an opening-cohort setting.

paper.title: DeXposure-Claw: An Agent System for DeFi Risk Supervision

author.affiliation: University of Edinburgh, University of Edinburgh

paper.abstract: Decentralized finance exposes supervisors to fast-moving, networked credit risks that are difficult to inspect directly from raw on-chain records. We present DeXposure-Claw, an end-to-end decision-support system that converts forecasts of future exposure networks into bounded, auditable review tickets. DeXposure-FM produces future graph distributions. Deterministic monitors and stress scenarios organize forecast signals into a typed EvidenceBundle, and an LLM turns this record into ranked tickets with evidence-linked rationales. Data-health and confidence controls restrict intervention-level outputs when the supporting evidence is insufficient, while supervisors retain final authority. DeXposure-Bench evaluates the resulting workflow across forecasting, warning, calibration, stress analysis, ticket construction, and degraded-input behavior. The release schema separates forecast evidence, queue position, and control state for supervisory review. Retained legacy tickets do not contain every designed gate field. Code: https://github.com/EVIEHub/DeXposure-Claw/tree/finnlp-2026-code-snapshot-v1.

paper.title: DelistBench: Evaluating Search-Enabled LLMs for Auditable Corporate-Event Database Completion
paper.abstract: Financial institutions need an independent way to detect missing, stale, and misclassified corporate-event records in vendor databases. We introduce Search-to-Record, a database-assurance task in which search-enabled large language models reconstruct institution-defined event records from public sources for a known security universe and historical cutoff, and DelistBench, a 1,200-record benchmark for security-level delisting announcements. We evaluate five models in paired closed-book and web-enabled conditions. Web access raises announcement-date accuracy within seven days by 34.0–48.0 percentage points and event-status accuracy by approximately 2.8–21.7 points; the best system achieves 81.5% overall joint accuracy within seven days. Economy web systems achieve 75.9–78.3% overall joint accuracy within seven days at 4.5–6.6% of the API cost of the most expensive web system. Risk-based triage identifies low-error subsets, although the highest-coverage operating point still sends 27.3% of the balanced test set to review. The evaluation identifies web retrieval as the main source of timing gains and shows that low-cost systems can approach the best system’s accuracy. Together, Search-to-Record, DelistBench, and the evaluation provide concrete deployment guidance: calibrate triage to local event prevalence and market mix, preserve positive-event recall, and route positive and ambiguous cases to targeted review. DelistBench is publicly available at https://github.com/tj-zyyyyyyy/DelistBench.

paper.title: DealTrace: Localizing and Intervening on Failures in Agentic Financial Reasoning
paper.abstract: Analyzing a financial deal is a long, multi-step task: an analyst reads a narrative memorandum against the Excel model behind it, rebuilds the forecast under the valuation, and writes a recommendation. LLM agents increasingly perform such work, but financial benchmarks measure isolated skills or final answers and do not show where a long analysis fails. We present DealTrace, a benchmark built on real deal packages, each pairing a confidential information memorandum with its financial model. A five-stage pipeline—extract, reconcile, project a masked forecast, assess market context, recommend—follows the analyst workflow; every clause of the recommendation cites the stage that produced it, and knockout and repair interventions attribute the outcome to individual stages. Across six frontier models, three scaffolding conditions, and four model judges, extraction, reconciliation, and grounding are reliable, and forecasting is the decisive stage: it is the strongest correlate of judged quality, the costliest stage to remove, and the only repair that improves every model, after which the models reach nearly the same score. Models flag discrepancies accurately but rarely use them in the verdict, a failure that outcome-level evaluation cannot detect. Scaffolding improves stage-level performance far more than the final score, and a critique pass adds cost without reliable gain. DealTrace evaluates the analysis process itself, not only its final answer.

paper.title: Topic-Aware Environmental Claim Extraction from Corporate News
paper.abstract: Corporate environmental claims frequently appear in news articles, providing an external view of sustainability-related communications. However, extracting such claims remains challenging as they are often implicit, distributed across multiple sentences, and embedded within narrative contexts. In this work, we propose an end-to-end system for automated environmental claim extraction enriched with contextual metadata. Our pipeline combines multi-label topic classification, topic-conditioned candidate claim-evidence extraction using large language models (LLMs), and candidate filtering with ASE-BERT, a lightweight aspect- and sentiment-aware classifier for claim detection. To support evaluation, we construct a curated dataset of corporate environmental news, annotated with claims, supporting evidence, and contextual attributes. Experimental results demonstrate that for claim classification, ASE-BERT attains the highest F1 (0.87) across the four combined environmental claim datasets, exceeding the best baseline without task-specific fine-tuning by 4 points. For end-to-end extraction, topic conditioning alone improves LLM F1 by an average of 15 points, and our full pipeline adds a further 5 points over the best topic-conditioned setting. These findings demonstrate that incorporating topic awareness and claim filtering substantially improves environmental claim extraction from corporate news, supporting downstream sustainability intelligence and decision-making tasks.

paper.title: Do Tools Matter, or Just Their Descriptions?
paper.abstract: Tool-augmented language models are increasingly applied to financial document reasoning, a setting that demands numerical precision over long financial filings. Earlier comparisons either mix up the model with its scaffolding or report tool-use gains without separating code, strategy, and environment. We isolate these factors in a controlled same-model ablation: six configurations share an identical GPT-5 backbone and differ only in the tool surface (callable tools plus their descriptions), with one control that additionally forces sub-model delegation. On DocMath-Eval under oracle context, the fully equipped configuration beats the restricted-tool baseline by +3.6 points (p=0.0028). Where this gain comes from matters more than its size: the system tools that give that configuration its name are used on under 0.2% of samples, and a description-only control, which describes the same tools but never runs them, performs almost identically (within 1 point on every split). The benefit comes from the tool descriptions, not from executing the tools. On long-document splits, the equipped model uses fewer iterations, has answers available earlier when runs are cut short, and varies its tool mix with document length. Comprehension errors dominate the hardest failures: the bottleneck is document comprehension, not the tool interface.

paper.title: Human Agreement and Return Association Are Not Interchangeable Criteria
paper.abstract: Financial NLP has a standard workflow: validate a sentiment tool against human labels, then trust it to extract market signal. This assumes the two evaluations measure the same thing. We test that assumption in a setting where both can be measured at once: a corpus of securities class actions (2002–2025) linking 70,500 X[formerly Twitter] messages to abnormal stock returns, with a single-annotator human labelled gold sample. Running five instruments (VADER, Loughran–McDonald, FinBERT, Twitter-RoBERTa, and an LLM annotator) through one identical pipeline, we find that the relationship between construct and predictive validity depends on the sampling convention and score representation. Under conventional method-specific sampling, human agreement aligns more closely with graded same-day associations than with one-day leads. On a fixed-n panel, however, agreement has similar graded rank correlations at both horizons, while the coarse ordering remains weak. Benchmark agreement therefore establishes semantic validity but does not by itself determine predictive rankings. In a conversation that is 17.6% spam, message volume predicts neither market damage nor settlement size.

paper.title: Bags of Words, Bags of Analysts: Two Event Spaces for Industry Classification

author.affiliation: University of New South Wales and University of Sydney, University of Sydney

paper.abstract: A company’s GICS sector can be inferred from what the firm writes about itself, and it can be inferred from who chooses to write about the firm. We show these are the same inference over two event spaces, and fit one multinomial naïve Bayes to both. In the first a company is a bag of the words of Item 1 of its 10-K; in the second it is a bag of the 814 analysts who covered it, with no use of what they wrote. Sector prototypes are counted log-probabilities in both cases, w_s = log p_s , so the two differ only in what is being counted.Over 426 S P 500 constituents the word space gives 83.7% top-1 recovery and the analyst space 73.7%, against a 16.2% majority-class baseline. Because the two spaces are conditionally independent given the sector their log-likelihoods simply add – but doing so captures only a quarter of the available gain (+0.75 points). A filing supplies some 2,100 wordevents against 18 analyst events at the median, and naïve Bayes counts each as independent, so the word log-likelihood varies across the eleven sectors with a median standard deviation of 766 nats against 8.3 for the analyst log-likelihood, a factor of 92: the sum is numerically dominated and analyst evidence rarely moves a decision. Standardising each log-likelihood within a company before adding removes the scale disparity and recovers +2.9 points [0.4, 5.4], reaching 86.5% top-1 and 94.8% top-2.A dense encoder is not better here, and not combinable on the same terms. Qwen3-Embedding-4B over the same filings reaches 76.9% under the nearest-centroid classifier that dense vectors admit, below naïve Bayes over the same words; and having no event counts it cannot form a third event space, so combining it means leaving the likelihood and choosing a scale.

paper.title: Market Signal Injection: Adversarial Context Manipulation of LLM Pricing Agents
paper.abstract: Large language model (LLM) pricing agents may respond to how market data is presented, even when its numerical values remain unchanged. We introduce market signal injection (MSI), an attack that manipulates numerical formatting, competitor ordering, or qualitative market commentary without issuing explicit instructions. We evaluate nine open-weight models in simulated Bertrand duopoly and triopoly markets and three proprietary models in duopoly markets. Sentiment-based attacks produce the largest behavioral shifts, which propagate to other firms and alter profits and consumer surplus. Susceptibility varies across model families, and larger models are not consistently more robust. Matched neutral-text controls and a rule-based agent support a framing-based account of these shifts under the fixed demand parameters of our simulation. Episode-held-out probes distinguish baseline from attacked activations in all eleven re-evaluated model–condition pairs: linear AUC is 1.00 and MLP AUC ranges from 0.93 to 0.99. This separability does not by itself identify harmful pricing decisions. Input canonicalization removes the tested sentiment attacks, while decision boundary anchoring, which combines prompt constraints with output projection, provides partial mitigation under the tested adaptive attacks. These results identify data presentation as an attack surface for LLM pricing agents and motivate defenses that account for interactions among agents.

paper.title: EVOQUANT: Self-Evolving Verifier-Guided Strategy Optimization for Robust Quantitative Trading

author.affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) and Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) and The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Quantitative strategy optimization remains largely manual, requiring domain experts to identify weak signals, tune risk-control rules, and repeatedly validate iterative revisions. Large language models can accelerate this process, but directly relying on them to rewrite trading strategies often introduces hallucinated edits, strategy drift, and back-test overfitting. We propose EVOQUANT, a self-evolving verifier-guided framework for strategy optimization in quantitative trading. Our method utilizes LLMs to deeply diagnose performance bottlenecks, generate semantically controlled candidate edits, select the best strategy through a multi-stage verification pipeline, and distill optimization experience into reusable knowledge for continual self-improvement. We evaluate our method using seven representative strategies: four from the A-share market and three from the crypto market.
