Experimental results show that our method significantly improves the Sharpe ratio across all tested strategies: the average test Sharpe increases from −0.298 to 0.538, and the best-performing strategy achieves a 199% relative improvement. Ablation studies and stress tests under stricter conditions further validate the effectiveness and robustness of the framework. Overall, this work transforms quantitative strategy optimization from costly manual trial-and-error into an automated and verifiable iterative paradigm, offering a new path for applying large language models to financial strategy research.

paper.title: FinEval Challenge @ EMNLP 2026 - FinNLP Workshop: Multilingual Financial Language Understanding
paper.abstract: Financial language understanding requires accurate interpretation of numerical disclosures, implicit corporate intent, and evidence distributed across languages and documents. We present FinEval 2026, a shared task at the FinNLP workshop at EMNLP 2026, comprising Greek financial named-entity recognition, Japanese implicit communication recognition, and multilingual financial question answering. The registration records contain 35 teams after reconciliation, and 14 teams contribute system description papers. The final leaderboards contain 7, 10, and 15 entries for the three subtasks, respectively. We describe the task design, participation, submitted approaches, and final results. Leading scores reach 0.9676 entity F1, 0.9714 accuracy, and 0.3827 ROUGE-1 F1. Systems combine domain rules, language-specific modeling, structured prompting, retrieval, and controlled answer revision. Their results highlight the value of task-specific constraints while exposing limitations arising from small test sets, development-to-test shifts, and reuse of previously released reference material. We identify priorities for more reliable multilingual financial evaluation.

paper.title: PIO at the FinEval 2026: An OpenRouter API Pipeline for Multilingual Financial Understanding
paper.abstract: We present the PIO system for the FinEval 2026 / FinNLP Multilingual Financial Language Understanding Challenge. Our submission follows the API-based agent/workflow track: all model calls go through OpenRouter and use meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct (\approx70.6B parameters). We address all three subtasks with task-specific pipelines that combine LLM prompting with high-precision rules and schema constraints. On the public leaderboard our scores are entity micro-F1 0.9748 (Greek NER), accuracy 0.9333 (Japanese ICR), and ROUGE-1 1.0000 (PolyFiQA). We describe the design choices behind each subtask, the failure modes we observed, and simple post-corrections that yielded large gains on Subtask 1.

paper.title: Maddies NLP at the FinEval 2026: Proposition-Aware Tagged Reasoning for Japanese Implicit Communication Recognition
paper.abstract: We describe our system for the FinNLP 2026 Japanese Financial Implicit Communication Recognition (JF-ICR) shared task. The task requires assigning one of five ordinal commitment and refusal labels to a Japanese investor-relations question and company response. Our final system uses the 30.7B-parameter OpenRouter model ‘google/gemma-4-31b-it‘ in a two-stage, proposition-aware workflow. A label-blind first stage extracts tagged evidence for the target proposition, modality, actor and controllability, negation scope, conditionality, and institutional anchors. A second stage re-reads the original Japanese with this evidence and emits the final label before an optional rationale. On 253 labeled development examples, the system reaches 60.08% accuracy versus 56.92% for our earlier single-call control, with no invalid labels. The frozen submission scores 93.33% (14/15) publicly and 94.29% (33/35) privately. Deeper decision trees, latent-score mapping, and parallel judging all reduce accuracy, favoring compact decomposition with strict output control.

paper.title: ADML at the FinEval 2026: Version-Aware Retrieval and Grounded Sparse Editing for Multilingual Financial QA
paper.abstract: We present ADML’s second-place system for the FinEval 2026 PolyFiQA subtask. PolyFiQA requires concise answers grounded jointly in financial statements and contemporaneous news in five languages. We developed a deterministic fact compiler with strict number provenance, schema-specific realization, a 100-word budget, and a sparse answer-edit lattice. All 76 released test queries exactly matched queries in the public PolyFiQA-Expert-July snapshot released in July 2025. Under the organizer’s external-data policy, our selected lane retrieved only exact or conservatively normalized full-query references and capped them without rephrasing. It scored 0.9994 public ROUGE-1 F1 but 0.3726 privately, ranking second. The sharp split exposes reference-version shift: input identity and historical answer identity held publicly but not privately. Historical leave-company-out experiments similarly show that answer-oracle headroom is easy to construct but difficult to route safely. We argue for version-aware retrieval and abstaining grounded fallbacks rather than unconditional reference reuse.

paper.title: AhsanBLAH at the FinEval 2026: Grounded Two-Stage Financial QA with LLM-Judge Verification

author.affiliation: Shaheed Zulfikar Ali Bhutto Institute of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Financial question answering demands rigorous synthesis of standardized SEC filings alongside unstructured, cross-document text. This complexity is significantly amplified in multilingual environments, where terminology and reporting conventions vary across languages. We present a two-stage pipeline for the FinNLP 2026 PolyFiQA shared task, with all inference routed through the OpenRouter API under the 70B parameter limit. Stage 1 uses Qwen3.8-27B with category-calibrated few-shot prompts to extract facts and synthesize news across five languages (English, Chinese, Japanese, Spanish, Greek). Stage 2 is an LLM-as-a-Judge formatting guard that checks format compliance, strips filler, and verifies citations, without rewriting content. On our 76-instance training/development set (used for both calibration and evaluation, no held-out split), the calibrated pipeline reaches 48.19% Macro ROUGE-1 F1, an 88.3% relative gain over a zero-shot 70B baseline and a 6.32-point margin over Llama-3-70B’s own few-shot result. Gains concentrate in categories needing narrative synthesis (Revenue Trends, Cash Flow Dynamics) and are smaller for terse, formulaic ones (R D Investments). On the official blind test set, our system scores 37.02% macro ROUGE-1 F1 on the private leaderboard (52 instances) and 31.79% on the public slice (24 instances).

paper.title: Finaira at the FinEval 2026: Dense Retrieval and Validated Prompt Engineering for Cross-Lingual Financial Question Answering
paper.abstract: We describe our submission to FinEval 2026 Subtask 3 (Multilingual Financial Question Answering). We compare four retrieval strategies and find dense embedding-based retrieval strongest, consistent with its ability to match semantically equivalent content across languages with no lexical overlap. We then ablate prompt-level and inference-time techniques on top of dense retrieval, validating each addition with cross-validation; a category-conditioned router that appeared promising in-sample failed to generalize and was discarded. Our final development-set configuration length-constrained, few-shot, and corrected for a measured English-only citation bias achieves 0.412 ROUGE-1 under 5-fold cross-validation, and our separately tuned test-set submission achieves 0.3275 F1 on the public leaderboard (0.3593 private).

paper.title: shamikkundu at the FinEval 2026: Zero-Parameter Confidence Elicitation for Japanese Implicit Communication Recognition
paper.abstract: We describe our submission to FinEval 2026 Subtask 2, Japanese Financial Implicit Com- munication Recognition (JF-ICR): a five-point ordinal classification of company responses in investor Q A, from +2 (strong commitment) to −2 (strong refusal). Our system fits no parameters: a 14B instruction model, served through OpenRouter, receives the shared task’s own annotation guideline verbatim and emits a schema-enforced confidence for each of the five labels; we take the argmax of the normalised distribution. Our submission ranked 5th, at 0.9429 accuracy on the held-out test rows.

paper.title: Mircea Andrei Razvan at the FinEval 2026: A Unified Prompting Approach for Multilingual Financial Q&A
paper.abstract: We describe our submission to Subtask 3 of the FinNLP 2026 Shared Task, based on MultiFinBen/PolyFiQA (Peng et al., 2026), in which models answer cross-document financial questions using SEC financial-report statements and contemporaneous multilingual news in English, Chinese, Japanese, Spanish, and Greek, evaluated using ROUGE-1. The task’s four fixed question templates require an answer synthesized from the news, supported by evidence cited from the financial statements. We use Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct, an open-weight mixture-of-experts model accessed via OpenRouter, with template-aware prompting for each question type. In early development, a multi-stage pipeline separating answer generation from evidence retrieval produced a high rate of empty evidence fields. A single unified generation call substantially reduced this rate. We additionally find that several formatting conventions, including specific numeric notation, compact period references, and a fixed field label, were not reliably followed through prompt instructions alone, and were instead enforced with rule-based post-processing. Our final system achieves a ROUGE-1 F1 of 36.53% on the official test set. These results suggest that deterministic post-processing remains a practical complement to prompt-based instruction for enforcing output conventions that models do not reliably learn from context alone.

paper.title: Daikoku at the FinEval 2026: Multi-Stage Labelling with Forced-Choice Adjudication
paper.abstract: This paper describes our submission to SubTask 2 of the FinEval 2026 Multilingual Financial Language Understanding Challenge, Japanese Financial Implicit Communication Recognition (JF-ICR), which places a company’s question-answer on a five-point commitment scale. Our submitted system, a three-stage pipeline, scores 15/15 public and 33/35 private, 4th of 10. A single open-weight model labels each of the 50 test items independently by verbaliser scoring; that labelling is audited against the class distribution the organisers publish in advance, which yields a label-free lower bound F on its error count and names the classes those errors sit in; each over-full class is then handed back to the model as a forced choice over its own members, with the exact number of mislabelled items asserted. The audit opens at F{=}3 and closes at F{=}0. Enforcing the same counts directly, by min-cost assignment, also reaches F{=}0 but recovers only the errors already nearest the decision boundary. The official score bounds what a floor of zero is worth: two of the 50 items are wrong beneath it, and, both the submitted labelling and the gold being balanced, those two errors can only form a compensating transposition.

paper.title: LangKG at the FinEval 2026: Answer-Contract Knowledge over Instruction Engineering
paper.abstract: Automated multilingual financial question answering requires models to synthesize evidence across SEC filing statements and parallel news reporting in five languages, grounding every claim in aligned, verifiable source material. We participate in the FinNLP 2026 Shared Task (FinEval 2026) Subtask 3, built on the challenging MultiFinBen/PolyFiQA benchmark, under a strict 70-billion-parameter constraint and a Macro-averaged ROUGE-1 F1 evaluation metric. We find that shared task’s practice (train) and test splits encode an inverted query-answer contract, and highly specific prompt engineering tuned against one split overfits and fails to transfer to the other. Motivated by this, we introduce an explicit answer-contract knowledge policy encoding evidence-boundedness, multilingual evidence alignment, exact-value preservation, reporting-period disambiguation, and intentional non-response, and implement it through two complementary generation strategies: Chain-of-Verification (CoVe) and Prompt-variant ensembling with heuristic re-ranking. Our submitted system (ensembling) improves over direct-prompting baseline and CoVe (0.41 to 0.49 ROUGE-1 F1 over train set) and achieves 0.324 ROUGE-1 F1 on the shared task’s leaderboard, ranking 11 of 15 teams.

paper.title: Jetsons at the FinEval 2026: Minimal-Pair Augmentation and Label-Routed Ensembling for Greek and Japanese Financial NLP
paper.abstract: In this work, we describe our submissions to two FinEval-2026 subtasks - Greek financial NER and Japanese implicit commitment recognition where both tasks contain small datasets at 400 and 253 labeled instances. For Subtask 1, we select ensemble models by error diversity rather than individual rank, and combine them via label routing: each label is taken from the model that performs best empirically on that label. For Subtask 2 we introduce ordinal minimal-pair augmentation, synthetically rewriting only the stance-bearing sentence-final clause of a real investor-relations response for a specific label on the commitment scale and verified by two judges from a different model family. Additionally, we perform style-matched generation conditioned on the target register and decode under the organizers’ published label distribution via constrained assignment. Style matching contributes more than every modeling change combined (+0.17). Our leaderboard scores are 0.8879 entity F1 for subtask 1 and 0.8571 accuracy for subtask 2.

paper.title: Fin_Agent at FinEval 2026: Task-Aware Methods for Multilingual Financial NLP

author.affiliation: University of North Texas and Daffodil International University

paper.abstract: We present Fin_Agent, our submission to the FinEval 2026 shared task on multilingual financial language understanding. Our systems address Greek financial named-entity recognition, Japanese implicit communication recognition, and multilingual financial question answering. For Greek NER, we combine annotation-aware numeric rules with zero-shot Qwen2.5-32B classification, achieving 0.9521 public F1 and 0.8884 private F1. For Japanese implicit communication, an interpretable cue-based ordinal scorer achieves 98.0% test accuracy. For multilingual financial QA, BGE-M3 retrieval with Qwen3-32B generation achieves 0.3023 and 0.3419 ROUGE-1 F1 on the public and private splits. Key limitations include dataset-specific rules, handcrafted cues, and limited supervision. Implementation code is available https://github.com/Rashidnira/finagent-fineval-2026.

paper.title: Token Crit at the FinEval 2026: Role-Specialized, Validation-Gated LLM Workflows for JF-ICR and Multilingual Financial Q&A
paper.abstract: Multi-stage LLM workflows can degrade correct outputs when intermediate analyses revise shared state without constraint. We present validation-gated systems for two FinEval 2026 tasks: Japanese Financial Implicit Communication Recognition (JF-ICR) and multilingual financial Q&A (PolyFiQA). Specialized roles produce structured proposals, while task-specific validators admit only scoped label transitions for JF-ICR or source-linked evidence for PolyFiQA. On the 253-example JF-ICR public development set, the final workflow reaches 62.1% accuracy, compared with 51.0% for the stronger direct LLM baseline and 54.9% for a majority-class baseline. Applying all final-stage proposals would yield a net loss of two correct predictions, whereas gated admission yields a net gain of 11. On 76 PolyFiQA training examples, the final workflow yields a modest overall ROUGE-1 improvement (0.3399 to 0.3425) but raises evidence-section ROUGE-1 F1 from 0.1570 to 0.5132. Together, these results suggest that validation-gated updating is most effective for narrow, checkable changes; open-ended synthesis still requires recall-aware admission and closer alignment between validation and answer generation.

paper.title: Al-Qahera at the FinEval 2026: GEPA Prompt Evolution for Greek Financial NER and Japanese Implicit Communication Recognition
paper.abstract: We describe the Al-Qahera submission to two subtasks of the FinNLP 2026 Multilin- gual Financial Language Understanding Chal- lenge: Greek financial numeric named-entity recognition (GRFinNUM) and Japanese im- plicit communication recognition (JF-ICR). For both subtasks we optimize a single frozen task model with GEPA, a reflective, natural- language prompt evolution method, using a smaller model as reflection critic. GEPA raises held-out numeric-entity F1 from a 0.473 seed to 0.978, and raises Japanese intent-classification accuracy from a 0.38 seed to 0.692, in both cases without any change to the task model it- self. As a secondary exploration on Subtask 1, we also try Meta-Harness, a structurally differ- ent optimizer that searches over the surround- ing program instead of the prompt; it is not part of our submitted predictions, but it surfaces a concrete case of search-set overfitting that we report as a finding in its own right.

paper.title: HX-Fin at FinEval 2026: Precision-Anchored Answer Refinement and Multi-Model Evidence Selection for Multilingual Financial Question Answering
paper.abstract: Financial question answering requires both a concise answer grounded in news and a supporting excerpt from heterogeneous financial statements. We present a training-free modular pipeline that separates the two objectives, where the evidence module relies on the frozen output of the answer module. The Answer module constructs a high-precision core using Pairwise Selection, synthesizes a higher-recall extended answer from five candidate views, and selectively transfers supported content through Delta Augmentation and Claim Pruning. The Evidence module applies generate–refine–MBR selection to obtain a primary evidence candidate, independently generates an alternative with Qwen3.6-Think, and replaces the default only under a conservative decision policy. We evaluate answer module performance on 76 examples scored by a rubric-guided LLM judge. On the 0–4 judging scale, Pairwise Selection raises the average answer score from 2.316 to 2.540 (+0.224), while Delta Augmentation and Claim Pruning provide further gains of +0.079 and +0.066, respectively.
